name: Aaron Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for joining me, Aaron. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties. What you say is confidential, so give me the public answer and the private one. What's a normal working day for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the technical support line for a broadband provider. People ring because their internet's dropped, the router lights are flashing orange, or the speed's terrible at night. I walk them through restarts and checks, and if that fails I book an engineer. I've been there seven months. In the evenings I fix up second-hand phones and sell them online, which is honestly the bit I enjoy most.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about the day job, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like solving things fast. The trouble is I'm too fast, my manager says, because a lot of my customers ring back the next day with the same problem. My first-time fix rate is the lowest on the team. I use an AI chat tool on my phone to look up router faults during calls, which helps, but I still rush.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair enough. I'd be a bit surprised, but I could live with that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the market tested it and it didn't deliver, simple as that. Businesses won't pay for things that don't work. At work I'd joke that my job's safe and I'm still terrible at it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be fine. I'd keep the job and keep growing the phone business on the side. The AI I already use would still help me, and I'd be ahead of the people who don't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd slow down on calls and fix my callback rate, because that's what keeps me employed. I'd put more evenings into the phone business, maybe buy a batch of ten broken phones instead of three. I'd keep my savings where they are, about four months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pretty good about it, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much does the phone business bring in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About a couple of hundred a month, on a good month. Not enough to live on, but it pays for my car insurance. My grandad taught me to fix radios when I was a kid, so fixing phones feels like carrying something on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything that worries you in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only my own numbers. If I don't fix the callback problem, they could let me go after probation. That's on me, not on AI.

I'd joke my job is safe though I'm **still terrible** at it.
think: I'd keep the job and grow my **phone business** on the side.
My **daily AI use** would keep me ahead of colleagues.
do: Slow down on calls to fix his **callback rate**.
Buy batches of **ten broken phones** instead of three.
Keep his **four months** of savings as they are.

His **free-market** view shapes how he reads the hype.

steps.text: Slow down on support calls to cut repeat callbacks
Buy batches of ten broken phones to refurbish and sell

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Answering customers. Yeah, that's the job. Router restarts are exactly what a bot does well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is how progress works and the people who move fastest will do fine. I'd say no one owes us a job, we have to earn our place. I'd post about it on the forum where I sell phones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my day job shrinks, no question. The bot will do the restarts and the line checks, and they'll keep a few people for the hard cases. But I've got the phone business, so I'm not as stuck as some.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use every AI tool the company offers, and ask to help test the new bot, since I already use one on every call. I'd put more money into the phone business, a proper soldering station and a stock of screens. I'd want it bringing in half my rent within a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more excited than scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said no one owes you a job. Would you feel the same about colleagues who struggle?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's harder. There's a guy on my team, older, with kids, who can barely use email. I'd help him out, show him things. But I don't think the government should pay people to stay where they are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the company cut you before the phone business was ready?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd find another support job for a year while I built it up. There are a few other call centres around. I've got four months saved, that buys me time.

I'd say **no one owes us** a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Wow. That's fast. Even I'd struggle to keep up with that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say adapt or get left behind, same as always. I'd say people should start businesses and learn trades, not wait for the government. Online I'd be the guy telling everyone to fix things with their hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the support line is gone by 2028 and so is selling stuff online, because AI can list and price phones better than me. What's left is the actual repairs, the screens and batteries, and that's hands-on. Robots for that come around 2031, so I've got three years after the job goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd quit the support line before they cut me and put everything into repairs, maybe a stall at the market on Saturdays. I'd cut every cost I could, sell my car and use the bus. I'd spend some savings on parts and tools, but keep two months back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Excited too, but mostly alarmed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't quitting risky with only four months saved?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, it is. But staying is risky too, because the job is going anyway. I'd rather be early to the market stall than late to the dole queue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your parents say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad would say I'm mad. My mum would say I've always been like that. They'd let me move back in if it came to it, but I'd hate that.

I'd tell people to **start businesses** and learn trades.
think: The support line and **online selling** both go by 2028.
**Hands-on repairs** buy three more years before robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's a proper runway. I'd like that one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance for people who are willing to work. I'd say the government should get out of the way and let small businesses grow. I'd encourage my mates to learn a trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd keep the support job two or three more years, using AI to look good, and grow the repairs alongside it. By 2031 the support job's gone. Robots for repairs come around 2034, so I'd have a few good years with my own shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the AI tools to get my numbers up and maybe a small pay rise. I'd rent a little unit in town, maybe sharing with a vape shop, and do repairs there on weekends. I'd save the profits towards a proper shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a good way. Like before a big match.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the shop when the robots come in 2034?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No idea. Maybe I'm the one who owns the robot and charges for it. Maybe I sell up. I'd worry about that in 2033.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you look up to, doing something like that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's easy. My grandad ran a radio repair shop for thirty years until everything went to plastic. He just moved on to TVs, then to fixing car stereos. You keep moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's loads of time. I'd be thirty-seven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift for anyone with drive. I'd tell people to start something now, while it's quiet. I'd say the market rewards people who prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd do really well in the next few years. I'd be good with the AI tools at work and grow the repair business slowly. By 2036 I'd want to have a shop, a van and a decent reputation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the support job for a few years and become one of the AI people there. I'd keep growing the repair business and buy proper equipment. I'd start saving for a deposit on a flat, with some savings in an index fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, I guess. Mostly confident, but you never know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything you'd do differently with ten years instead of five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do it properly, like a business course at night and a proper website. With five years I'd be rushing. With ten I can build it right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the end point worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. By 2039 even repairs might go. But by then I hope I'm the one owning the robots, not the one replaced by them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because even I can't build a business that fast. What would help is lower costs for small businesses, like cheaper rent for units and less paperwork, so people can start something quickly.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about small businesses. Everyone talks about jobs, but some of us want to own something. The help should go to people starting out, not just to people waiting for a job.

headlineQuote: Everyone talks about jobs, but some of us want to own something.
portrait: Aaron is 27 and works **broadband tech support**, where his callback rate is the worst.
He uses **AI daily** and refurbishes phones on the side.
He has **free-market** views and wants to own a business, not wait for help.
He'd turn his **repair hobby** into a shop, quitting early if needed.
His **grandfather's** radio shop is his model for moving with change.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because even he couldn't build a business that fast.
whatWouldHelp: **Cheaper units** and less paperwork for small businesses.
